newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's new government says "the party is over".
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's new government says "the party is over".

text.p: Interim President Fabian Alarcon's new administration said on Wednesday "the party is over" after six months of rule by populist Abdala Bucaram and vowed to put the country's economic house in order.
"Ecuadoreans have woken up from six months of bad dreams," top government official Arturo Gangotena said.
"After a six-month party, we have to start looking into the state of the accounts," Gangotena, whose job is similar to that of presidential chief of staff, told a local television station.

Ecuador's Congress on Tuesday night appointed its leader, Alarcon, as president until August 1998, ending a bizarre political crisis sparked by the ouster of Bucaram on grounds of "mental incompetence." His colourful rule ended amid reports of rampant corruption and nepotism.

In his first words as interim president, Alarcon, 49, pledged to introduce a new style in politics because Ecuadoreans were tired of "insults, bad manners and arrogance," a clear reference to Bucaram's abrasive style.
"Instability is over, now comes time to work ... we're going to restore dignity to this country ... and respect between government and governed," he said.
Anticipating belt-tightening measures, he asked people to be prepared for sacrifices, describing the economic situation as "catastrophic."

One of his first acts on Wednesday was to repeal unpopular measures contained in an austerity package launched by Bucaram last month. Those programmes sparked a national strike that contributed to his downfall.
His plan included cuts in state subsidies and increases in electricity and gas rates of up to 200 percent. Telephone rates jumped 600 percent.
Alarcon said he would detail his economic plans in a few days but analysts saw a bumpy road ahead and predicted the fiscal deficit was likely to be a major headache.

"The main problem is going to be the fiscal deficit because of the rolling back of the economic measures ... which will translate into a loss of $600 million for the state," analyst and banker Diego Lavalle said.

From a projected 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, most analysts see the deficit widening to between 5 and 7 percent of GDP. Inflation, at 25.5 percent in 1996, could hit 38 percent this year, with the economy growing 1.5 to 2 percent, down from the previous government's forecast of up to 5 percent.
After a four-day carnival holiday and a somewhat surreal episode, with three people at one point claiming the presidency, Ecuador returned to a semblance of normality.
The nation's attention focused on its national soccer team which routed Uruguay 4-0 in a World Cup qualifying game in Quito. Alarcon was present at the match.
Meanwhile, Bucaram continued to proclaim from abroad that he was the legitimate, constitutional president of Ecuador.
In Panama, where he slammed Alarcon as "a traitor, a Judas," he repeated that he was deposed in a disguised coup that was a bad sign for democracy in the region.

"The Latin American community wants no such Pandora's box ... that could turn into a habit," he told Colombia's Caracol radio network. "If Bucaram does not go back it will set a bad example and we'll have dictatorships in all countries."
His unceremonious ouster was a "congressional coup," he said, adding he could have easily engineered the same trick. "I can get 100 friends, $10 million and buy off 10 of these rats," he said.

Bucaram, who left Ecuador on Tuesday on a regional tour to win support, was scheduled to arrive in Buenos Aires on Thursday. He received backing from Argentine President Carlos Menem -- of Arab descent like him -- who said Alarcon was a "de facto" ruler and Argentina would not attend his inauguration.
